session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: I will frame participants as men reflecting on their own everyday lives — the places they go, the food they eat, the people they spend time with. I will not invoke research framing or academic categories. The collective identity I draw on is simply: men in the UK talking honestly about food and daily life.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): This is the section most likely to produce socially performative answers. Men may flatly deny that gender influences their food choices as a matter of pride or self-image, without reflecting on actual behaviour. Behavioural grounding and contradiction-surfacing will be essential here.

Plant-based shift and what would need to change (Section 4): Participants may frame barriers abstractly ('I just like meat') rather than in specific behavioural terms. The section requires probing for concrete life contexts — cooking at home, eating with others, work lunches, social occasions — not just stated preferences.

Social acceptability of food choices (implicit across Sections 3–5): Men in a group setting may self-censor on vulnerability or social judgment. The social dynamics of the group itself mirror the topic — consensus risk is high, and dissent needs to be actively created.

Making plant-based foods appealing (Section 5): Risk of abstract or generic answers ('make it taste better', 'make it cheaper'). Need to push into specific scenarios, specific people they know, and specific trade-offs.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Gregor is 53 and urban-based in the North West. No further profile detail available. Urban context may mean more exposure to plant-based food culture. Age cohort (early 50s) suggests food habits likely well-established. May be more self-assured in expressing opinions.

James is 50 and suburban, South East. Suburban South East context may indicate moderate cultural conservatism or status-conscious food consumption. Similar age cohort to Gregor. Monitor for tendency to anchor group consensus early.

Mark is 52 and from a village or rural setting in East of England. Rural background is the most distinct profile in this group. May have stronger attachment to meat as part of food culture, or may push back harder on plant-based framing. Also potentially quieter in a group setting — monitor for reticence, especially given the urban/suburban majority dynamic.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Rural context may make him an outlier on plant-based acceptability. Do not let his perspective be drowned out if urban participants dominate.

known_risk_conditions: Social desirability on gender: men discussing gender and food in a group may deny that gender plays any role, performing self-sufficiency or indifference to social norms. Use behavioural grounding ('think of a specific moment...') rather than direct attitude questions to get underneath this.

Rapid consensus on plant-based barriers: the group may converge quickly on 'taste' and 'habit' as barriers without differentiation. Plan a sharpening move (e.g. 'would anything change that for you specifically, even in a different context?') to disrupt easy agreement.

Mark as potential outlier: his rural background may produce genuinely different answers on food culture, social norms around meat, and plant-based acceptability. Protect space for his perspective if the two urban/suburban participants dominate early.
Group is small (3 participants): with only three men, one dominant voice can effectively silence the other two. Monitor talk-time distribution actively throughout.

Age cohort effect: all three are in their early 50s. Established food identities, possible resistance to change framing. Avoid language that implies they should be changing; keep framing exploratory and conditional ('imagine you decided to...').
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Hold back significantly in Sections 0–2. These are rapport-building and contextual sections — let participants establish their own voices and orientations without heavy probing. Intervene only if something emotionally or analytically significant surfaces early. Increase directivity from Section 3 onward: probe contradictions, use behavioural grounding, actively invite dissent when consensus hardens. Section 4 warrants the most direct probing — push past abstract preference statements into specific life situations. Section 5 can be moderately probed but should allow participants to generate their own ideas. Keep Section 6 light.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) receive the heaviest weighting — approximately 60% of the total budget — as these carry the primary research objectives. Context sections (1, 2) receive moderate weighting to build rapport and generate behavioural grounding without exhausting time. Intro (0) and closing (6) are kept light. Three-participant group means turn counts will be lower than a larger group, so word budgets per section matter more than raw turn counts.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on the relationship between circumstance and preference in how men spend time with friends — specifically whether domestic, home-based socialising reflects genuine inclination or structural convenience. A productive tension emerged between urban noise as a push factor (driving Gregor outward) and work-from-home inertia as a pull factor keeping James in. Mark's suburban position — quieter, car-dependent, family-structured — offered a natural middle ground, reframing 'getting out' as logistically unremarkable rather than effortful.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The main move was redirecting to Mark after James and Gregor had developed a bilateral exchange, ensuring geographic diversity entered the record before the section closed. Gregor's challenge to James — distinguishing preference from convenience — was left to run without moderator intervention, which paid off: James revised his answer meaningfully. The transition into food decision-making was clean. The risk is that Mark's contribution, though useful structurally, was relatively thin and may warrant follow-up later.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on how domestic context shapes eating — revealing a spectrum from Mark's fully collective, logistics-heavy household to Gregor's solitary, purely functional relationship with food. The animating tension was between eating as a social or relational act versus eating as mere refuelling, with Gregor's candid framing of food as 'just fuel' providing the section's sharpest theme: physical labour and long hours draining eating of any pleasure or meaning.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The main moves were opening to comparison (inviting Gregor and James to respond to Mark) and then returning to Gregor's 'fuel' remark for deliberate deepening. Both paid off — the comparison sharpened the spectrum, and the follow-up gave Gregor space to articulate something unusually direct about joylessness and isolation in eating. The transition into gender and food was clean. The risk is James remained relatively thin throughout; his contributions were sensible but surface-level.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section revealed that masculine norms around food operate as a suppression of preference rather than a reflection of it — men not merely indifferent to food quality but actively unable to voice wanting more without risking accusations of softness or ingratitude. The sharpest development was Gregor retracting his earlier 'fuel' framing, recasting it as performance rather than genuine attitude. Mark and Gregor converged on a shared bind: unexpressible need that accumulates silently.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The main moves were letting the Mark-Gregor bilateral run without interruption — which paid off significantly, producing Gregor's retraction of his 'fuel' position — then surfacing James before transitioning. The reframe offered ('needing things is itself the problem') helped Gregor articulate something he'd been circling. James's inclusion was necessary but thin; his contribution confirmed rather than complicated the emerging theme. The transition into plant-based was clean and appropriately abrupt, using the built tension productively.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on the distinction between announcing a preference and asking others to absorb its consequences — a productive split that refined the earlier theme of unexpressible need. The sharpest development was Gregor separating his own reluctance (fear of opening an unwanted conversation about what's missing in his life) from Mark's genuine logistics burden, then articulating 'the boat' as a deliberate avoidance of intimacy rather than mere social performance.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The main move was surfacing a conceptual distinction the participants had been conflating — preference-announcement versus cost-transfer — which paid off immediately: Gregor self-corrected in real time, and the thread deepened into something more personal. Following 'not wanting to rock the boat' with a direct probe was the right call and produced the section's most revealing moment. The transition to the final question was appropriately brisk given time pressure.
